title: M6 Pro Chip Geekbench Scores Suspected Fake, Says MacRumors: What’s the Truth?
body:
Apple’s upcoming M‑series silicon has once again become the subject of heated speculation after a purported Geekbench benchmark for the unreleased “M6 Pro” chip surfaced online. The performance numbers, which claim a dramatic leap over the current M2‑based lineup, have been quickly called into question by Geekbench’s own creator, John Poole, who says the data contains internal inconsistencies that strongly suggest the results are fabricated. The incident underscores the challenges that tech enthusiasts and journalists face in verifying hardware claims in an environment where rumors spread rapidly across social media and niche forums.

The alleged benchmark appeared on a popular technology forum earlier this week, accompanied by a screenshot that displayed single‑core and multi‑core scores far exceeding those of Apple’s latest M2 Pro and M2 Max processors. According to the post, the M6 Pro would deliver roughly a 40 percent increase in single‑core performance and an even larger boost in multi‑core throughput, positioning it as a game‑changing step for Mac laptops and desktops. The thread quickly attracted attention, with users sharing the image and speculating on Apple’s future roadmap, which has so far been tightly guarded since the company announced the M2 family in early 2022.

John Poole, the founder of the Geekbench benchmarking suite, responded to inquiries from journalists by conducting a detailed review of the posted results. He identified several red flags: the score distribution did not align with the known scaling patterns of Apple’s silicon, the reported hardware identifier was inconsistent with Apple’s naming conventions, and the test environment appeared to be configured in a way that would be impossible on an actual Mac device. Poole also noted that the benchmark’s timestamp predates the rumored silicon’s expected release window, further eroding its credibility. In a brief statement, he warned readers that the image was likely a fabricated or heavily edited representation, urging the community to treat such unverified data with skepticism.

The episode is not the first time that bogus performance claims have circulated in the Apple ecosystem. Over the past few years, several “leaked” benchmark sheets have made the rounds, often originating from anonymous sources on platforms like Reddit, 4chan, and Discord. While some leaks have later proven accurate—such as early performance previews of the M1 and M2 chips—others have been debunked after careful analysis. The proliferation of AI‑generated images and deep‑fake technology has only amplified the difficulty of distinguishing genuine data from counterfeit. For journalists, the incident highlights the importance of cross‑checking claims with multiple independent sources and, when possible, obtaining direct verification from the benchmark developers or the hardware manufacturer.

Industry analysts note that the hype surrounding an “M6 Pro” is understandable, given Apple’s aggressive cadence of silicon upgrades and the competitive pressure from rivals like Intel and AMD, which are also racing to deliver higher‑performance cores for laptops and workstations. However, the absence of any official roadmap or confirmation from Apple means that any performance speculation remains just that—speculation. If Apple were indeed working on a next‑generation chip that dramatically outpaces the M2 series, it would likely be unveiled alongside a new Mac lineup at a major Apple event, complete with validated benchmarks and real‑world performance testing.

Looking ahead, the incident serves as a cautionary tale for both consumers and media outlets eager for the next big performance leap. As Apple continues to push the boundaries of its in‑house silicon, the demand for early data will persist, but the responsibility to verify that data rests squarely on the shoulders of the reporting community. Readers should await official announcements and independently verified benchmarks before drawing conclusions about the capabilities of any future M‑series processor. Until Apple provides concrete details, the M6 Pro will remain a phantom in the rumor mill, and the industry will watch closely for the next authentic glimpse of Apple’s silicon roadmap.
